title: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (3 of 7)
hook: you wake up from a dream where your wallet was stolen; do you call the police?
tomorrow: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (4 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rope and the snake. The fear was real, the snake was borrowed, and the cure was a lamp. Your line: not two.

Last night, in a dream, someone stole your wallet. You chased them through a market that was also somehow your old school. You woke up furious, heart still racing. Do you call the police? Of course not. You check the nightstand, the wallet's there, and you go make coffee. But here's the strange part: while you were dreaming, the theft was completely real to you. Nothing in the dream told you it was a dream. Advaita teachers ask: what if waking life is real in the same way?
screen: `A WALLET STOLEN IN A DREAM.` → `DO YOU CALL THE POLICE?` → `REAL, WHILE IT LASTED.`

segments.voice: People hear Advaita and think it says the world is an illusion, nothing matters, so why bother? That's not what the teachers say. Later Advaita thinkers, building on Shankara, sorted reality into three levels, and it clears up a lot. First, the level of the snake on the rope, or the dream: things that seem real only while you're mistaken, and vanish when you look closely. Second, the everyday level: rent and traffic and your mother's birthday. This is fully real for all practical purposes. Here, cause and effect hold, promises matter, cruelty hurts, and duty is duty. Third, the absolute level: Brahman alone, not two. So is the world real or not? Advaita's answer is a careful word: mithya. Not simply unreal, like a square circle. Not independently real, like Brahman. Something in between: real as long as it's there, and depending on something deeper for its being, the way the snake depends on the rope, and the dream on the dreamer. So Advaita doesn't excuse you from anything. Tradition remembers Shankara himself walking across India, debating in public, founding monasteries and writing devotional hymns. You still pay the rent. You still keep your word. What changes is the grip. The dream is taken seriously while it's on, and it doesn't own you. The wallet matters. The theft in the dream doesn't follow you into the kitchen.
screen: `THE SNAKE AND THE DREAM.` · `THE EVERYDAY: RENT, TRAFFIC, DUTY.` · `BRAHMAN ALONE, NOT TWO.` · `MITHYA: REAL, BUT NOT ON ITS OWN.` · then, large: `NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Remember a recent dream, even a scrap of one, and how real it felt at the time; then notice where it appeared, in awareness, the same awareness that's here now. Notice this room, this body, this moment, also appearing, and don't decide anything about it. Just feel the one awareness that holds last night's dream and this room now.
Advaita and its three levels: the dream or the snake, the everyday world, and Brahman alone. The world is mithya: fully real to live in, not real on its own.
Your line: not two. Real enough to live in, just not real on its own. That's day two eighty-three.

howItsDone: Advaita teachers explain the world as mithya, dependent reality, and distinguish levels of reality (the apparent, the practical and the absolute) so that students keep ethics and duty fully in place while contemplating non-duality.

fork.reveal: the theft was real in the dream and doesn't follow you out. Advaita says waking to Brahman is something like that, while the everyday stays fully in force meanwhile.

original.note: Sanskrit: mithya, usually translated 'false' or 'illusory'; in Advaita, dependent reality, neither real on its own nor simply unreal.

trapdoor: what you thought: Advaita means the world isn't real.
what it means: the world is mithya: real to live in, but depending on Brahman for its being, like a dream on a dreamer.

what a scholar hears: the three levels (pāramārthika, vyāvahārika, prātibhāsika) are systematized by post-Shankara Advaitins; mithya is defined as 'other than real and unreal' (sad-asad-vilakṣaṇa), and whether Shankara himself held this exact scheme is debated.
